projects.story:
The online shop customers actually see: product listings, filters, the cart and a three-step checkout. Pages are server-rendered, with a thin layer of TypeScript for the interactive parts.

Conversion dipped after the last redesign. Support is fielding tickets about prices, promo codes and a search box that feels sluggish, and an accessibility audit came back with a long list.

## What you'll work on

- Formatting money and other values the way customers expect to read them
- Form behaviour, validation and accessible markup
- Small performance fixes in the browser, like debouncing input

## Good fit if you

- Build user interfaces, or want to get sharper at the details that make one feel solid
- Are comfortable with **JavaScript**, **TypeScript** or plain **HTML**
- Care what a bug looks like from the customer's side of the screen

Stack: TypeScript, JavaScript, HTML.

projects.title: Accounts API
projects.summary: Backend: sign-up, login and account endpoints behind every app.
projects.story:
The service every client talks to for sign-up, login, sessions and password resets. Most of it is Go, a few older endpoints are still PHP, the admin back office is a small Ruby app, the password service is Java, and the login gateway in front is TypeScript.

It mostly works, and the on-call channel has opinions about the rest: list endpoints that accept any page size, reset links that expire too soon, and logs that are hard to search during an incident.

## What you'll work on

- Parsing and validating request parameters with sensible defaults
- Time and expiry logic, where off-by-one and unit mix-ups hide
- Rate limiting and log handling for the people on call

## Good fit if you

- Write backend services, or want practice with the bugs they actually get
- Like **input validation**, edge cases and reading a stack trace at 2am
- Know **Go**, **PHP**, **Ruby**, **Java** or **TypeScript**, or want to try one of them on familiar problems

Stack: Go, PHP, Ruby, Java, TypeScript.

projects.title: Data platform
projects.summary: Data: nightly partner imports, cleaning and the reports finance relies on.
projects.story:
Partners drop CSV exports in a bucket every night. A pipeline cleans them, loads the warehouse and feeds the reports finance reads on Monday morning.

The exports are messier than anyone admits: quoted commas in company names, duplicate customers with slightly different emails, and orders that never got paid. When the numbers look wrong, this is where people come asking.

## What you'll work on

- Parsing awkward input files without losing data
- Cleaning and deduplicating records before they reach the warehouse
- SQL for the reports and reconciliations people rely on

## Good fit if you

- Work with data, or are the person on your team who ends up writing the SQL
- Enjoy turning messy input into something you can trust
- Know **Python**, **SQL** or **C#**, or want more practice with them

Stack: Python, SQL, and C# for the billing jobs.

projects.title: Edge proxy
projects.summary: Systems: the low-latency proxy in front of everything.
projects.story:
A small proxy in front of everything: it terminates connections, caches hot responses and exports latency metrics. The hot path is C and C++; the control plane and metrics are Go.

Every allocation shows up on a flame graph here. The backlog is about doing more with fixed memory, measuring the right thing, and keeping configuration readable for whoever is paged.

## What you'll work on

- Fixed-size data structures such as ring buffers and LRU caches
- Latency percentiles and the metrics behind dashboards
- Small, strict configuration formats

## Good fit if you

- Do systems or performance work, or want to get closer to the metal
- Think about memory, ordering and what happens under load
- Know **C**, **C++** or **Go**, or are learning one of them

Stack: C, C++, Go.

Since the IPv6 listener went live on Tuesday, every request that addresses the proxy by its v6 literal gets the default vhost's **421 Misdirected Request**. The health checker on `[2001:db8::1]:8080` has been red since; on-call silenced it at 02:10.

```text
421 GET http://[2001:db8::1]:8080/healthz host="[2001" vhost=default
421 GET http://[2001:db8::1]/healthz      host="["     vhost=default
```

`normalize_host(host, out, size)` in `src/normalize_host.c` turns a Host header into the name routing and the cache key use. It writes it to `out` and returns its length, or `-1` when the value is not a host (`null` in the checks). The rules are in `docs/vhosts.md`: lowercase, no port, no trailing dot, and an IPv6 literal keeps its brackets and loses only the port after them. A literal that is never closed, or is followed by anything other than a port, is not a host. Plain hostnames already work and must keep working.

docs/vhosts.md.text:
# Virtual hosts

Each request is routed on its Host header after `normalize_host` (src/normalize_host.c) has
normalized it. The cache key uses the same value, so two spellings of one host share entries.

## Normalizing

- Lowercase: `Shop.Example.COM` → `shop.example.com`.
- No port: `shop.example.com:8443` → `shop.example.com`.
- No trailing dot: `shop.example.com.` → `shop.example.com`.
- An IPv6 literal keeps its brackets and loses only the port after them:
  `[2001:db8::1]:8080` → `[2001:db8::1]`. A literal that is never closed, or is followed by
  anything other than a port, is not a host.
- A value with nothing left is not a host.

Anything that is not a host gets the default vhost's 421.

## Config (edge.conf, excerpt)

```text
vhost shop.example.com   { upstream shop; }
vhost cdn.example.com    { upstream static; }
vhost [2001:db8::1]      { upstream shop; }    # v6 listener, health checks
default                  { return 421; }
```

The season report fails as soon as it reaches the sheets from the Oregon volunteers:

```text
  File "notebook/units.py", line 9, in to_mm
    return float(value) * MM_PER[unit]
KeyError: 'in'
```

Their sheets differ from ours in three ways:

- lengths in inches (`0.6 in`), and sometimes no space or a capital unit (`12mm`, `1.3 CM`, `0.5in`);
- lots nobody measured have the length left blank, or a `?` when the volunteer wasn't sure.

`length_report(lines)` in `notebook/report.py` gives, per species, the number of lots measured and the shortest, longest and mean length in millimetres, each rounded to one decimal. An inch is 25.4 mm. Unmeasured lots don't count towards any of those numbers, but their species still appears: with no measured lot it shows `measured: 0` and `None` for the lengths.

"""Notebook lines, as typed up from the paper field notebook. One line per specimen lot:

    2026-06-03 | Ridge B | Carabus nemoralis | 14.5 mm | 2

date | site | species | body length | individuals in the lot. The length is left blank when
nothing was measured.
"""

FIELDS = ("date", "site", "species", "length", "count")


def fields(line):
    """The five fields of a line, stripped, as written."""
    parts = [part.strip() for part in line.split("|")]
    if len(parts) != len(FIELDS):
        raise ValueError(f"expected {len(FIELDS)} fields: {line!r}")
    return parts

"""Lengths as written in the notebook, converted to millimetres. The label printer uses
to_mm too."""

MM_PER = {"mm": 1, "cm": 10}


def to_mm(text):
    """'14.5 mm' or '1.2 cm' in millimetres."""
    value, unit = text.split()
    return float(value) * MM_PER[unit]

Support merges duplicate accounts by hand, and it is always the same story: someone signs up as `Jane.Doe@Example.com`, forgets, and signs up again a month later as `jane.doe@example.com ` from their phone. Sign-up compares addresses exactly as typed, so it never finds the first account.

`CanonicalEmail(raw)` in `canonical_email.go` should return the key sign-up looks accounts up by, and `ok` false for anything we don't accept as an address:

- Surrounding whitespace is ignored. Whitespace anywhere inside the address makes it invalid.
- An address has exactly one `@`, with something on both sides of it.
- The whole address is lowercased: every provider our users are on treats the local part case-insensitively.
- For **gmail.com** and **googlemail.com** (those exact domains, nothing else), dots in the local part are dropped, so is everything from the first `+` on, and the domain becomes `gmail.com`. Other domains keep their dots and `+` tags as they are: plenty of mail servers deliver `+` addresses to different people.
- If the Gmail rules leave the local part empty, the address is invalid.

def normalize_email(email):

> Ridge B shows 6 lots. We have 19 on paper, I counted them twice. And Alder Creek's first visit says June 14, but we set the traps there on May 28.

`site_summary(lines)` gives, per site: the number of lots, the individuals across them, the number of distinct species, and the earliest (`first`) and latest (`last`) date the site appears. Dates are written `YYYY-MM-DD`.

We go back to the same sites all season, and pages are often typed up days late, so the export is in the order lines were typed, not by site or by date. It needs to stay fast: going back to rescanning the notebook for every site is not an option.

notebook/labels.py.text:
"""Notebook lines, as typed up from the paper field notebook. One line per specimen lot:

    2026-06-03 | Ridge B | Carabus nemoralis | 14.5 mm | 2

date | site | species | body length | individuals in the lot. The length is left blank when
nothing was measured.
"""

FIELDS = ("date", "site", "species", "length", "count")


def fields(line):
    """The five fields of a line, stripped, as written."""
    parts = [part.strip() for part in line.split("|")]
    if len(parts) != len(FIELDS):
        raise ValueError(f"expected {len(FIELDS)} fields: {line!r}")
    return parts


def parse_line(line):
    """A line as a dict: every field as written, the count as a number."""
    row = dict(zip(FIELDS, fields(line)))
    row["count"] = int(row["count"])
    return row

notebook/sites.py.text:
"""Per-site totals for the season summary."""
from itertools import groupby

from notebook.labels import parse_line


def site_summary(lines):
    """Per site: lots, individuals, distinct species, and the first and last date it was
    visited."""
    # One pass instead of rescanning the notebook for every site: the export is in notebook
    # order, so each site's lines come together.
    rows = [parse_line(line) for line in lines]
    summary = {}
    for site, group in groupby(rows, key=lambda row: row["site"]):
        group = list(group)
        summary[site] = {
            "lots": len(group),
            "individuals": sum(row["count"] for row in group),
            "species": len({row["species"] for row in group}),
            "first": group[0]["date"],
            "last": group[-1]["date"],
        }
    return summary

-- Finance's collected-by-partner report: what each partner's customers have paid us.
-- orders(id, partner, total), payments(id, order_id, amount)
SELECT o.partner, SUM(o.total) AS collected
FROM orders o
JOIN payments p ON p.order_id = o.id
GROUP BY o.partner
ORDER BY collected DESC;

Mateo replaced the response cache's `std::unordered_map` index with an open-addressing table on Thursday (#412, notes in `docs/412-cache-index.md`) to take the per-insert allocation off the hot path. CPU at peak is down 9%, but since the deploy:

- the cache hit ratio went from **94.1%** to **71.3%**, worst on the PoPs that purge the most;
- origin requests are up **3.2×**;
- `edgectl cache get` reports misses for keys whose responses are visibly in the arena.

```text
14:02:11 purge key=3                        ok
14:02:19 get   key=11  miss                 (arena slot 4: key=11, age 41s)
14:02:19 get   key=19  miss                 (arena slot 5: key=19, age 38s)
```

`cache_index(slots, ops)` in `src/cache_index.cpp` replays a cache log against an index of `slots` slots: `["put", key, value]`, `["get", key]` and `["erase", key]` (a purge). It returns what each get found, `-1` for a miss. The index must behave like a map of at most `slots` entries: a get finds the latest value put under its key unless the key was purged since, and a put is refused (the response is served uncached) only when every slot holds a live entry. A purged response must never come back. Keep the flat table: going back to a node-based map is not the fix.

# #412: open-addressing cache index

Author: Mateo O. Merged Thursday, deployed to every PoP by 14:00.

## Why

The response cache's index was a `std::unordered_map<int, int>`: one heap node per insert. At
peak that was 9% of CPU on the edge flame graphs, most of it in `operator new` and `free`.

## What

A flat array of `cache.index_slots` slots, allocated once at startup. A key's home slot is
`key % slots`; on a collision, the next slot, wrapping around at the end (linear probing).
A lookup walks from the home slot until it finds the key or reaches an empty slot. When every
slot holds an entry, a new response is served without being cached.

## Results (canary PoP, 24 h)

- CPU at peak: -9.2%
- p99 time to first byte: 3.1 ms → 2.6 ms
- Allocations per request on the cache path: 1 → 0

# Edge proxy

A small proxy in front of everything: it terminates connections, caches hot responses and exports latency metrics. The hot path is C and C++; the control plane and metrics are Go.

Every allocation shows up on a flame graph here. The backlog is about doing more with fixed memory, measuring the right thing, and keeping configuration readable for whoever is paged.

## What you'll work on

- Fixed-size data structures such as ring buffers and LRU caches
- Latency percentiles and the metrics behind dashboards
- Small, strict configuration formats

## Good fit if you

/**
 * Session rules for the login gateway, as signed off by security (SEC-118).
 *
 * A login starts a session family. A client refreshes with the family's current refresh token
 * and gets the next one; each refresh token works once. A refresh is decided in this order:
 *
 *   1. A token that is not in the family: sign in again ("unknown").
 *   2. A revoked family (signed out everywhere, password changed): sign in again ("revoked").
 *   3. A family SESSION_LIFETIME_MS or more after its login: sign in again ("expired").
 *   4. A token that was already rotated:
 *      - up to REFRESH_GRACE_MS after its rotation (inclusive), the client lost a race with
 *        itself: answer with the family's current token and issue nothing new;
 *      - any later, someone else has a copy: sign in again ("reuse") and revoke the family.
 *   5. Otherwise rotate: issue the family's next token.
 *
 * Only "reuse" revokes the family: every token in it stops working, the current one included.
 */

/** Mobile sessions last 30 days from login, however often they refresh. */
export const SESSION_LIFETIME_MS = 30 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000;

/** How long a just-rotated token is still answered, for clients that refresh twice at once. */
export const REFRESH_GRACE_MS = 10 * 1000;

pipeline/readers.py.text:
import csv
import io

from pipeline.money import to_cents

KINDS = {"sale", "refund", "adjustment"}


def read_settlements(text):
    """The rows of a partner settlement export, and how many rows were rejected.

    Each row has partner, order, kind, currency and amount: signed cents, as the partner
    wrote them. These rows are also loaded into raw_settlements as they are. A row that can't
    be read is rejected (counted and left out) rather than guessed at.
    """
    rows = []
    rejected = 0
    for raw in csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(text)):
        kind = raw["type"].strip().lower()
        if kind not in KINDS:
            rejected += 1
            continue
        try:
            amount = to_cents(raw["amount"])
        except ValueError:
            rejected += 1
            continue
        rows.append({
            "partner": raw["partner"].strip(),
            "order": raw["order_id"].strip(),
            "kind": kind,
            "currency": raw["currency"].strip().upper(),
            "amount": amount,
        })
    return rows, rejected

# Weighted balancing

Status: agreed, for the origin-v2 canary. Owner: Mateo.

`server <name> weight=<n>;` gives a server n shares of an upstream's requests. `weight=0`
drains it: it keeps its place in the block but gets no requests. An upstream whose servers
are all drained has nowhere to send a request.

## Smooth, not bursty

With 5:1:1 a naive scheme sends five requests in a row to the first server. We do what nginx
does instead, so the small server's requests are spread out:

1. Every server starts with a current value of 0.
2. For each request, add each server's weight to its current value.
3. Pick the server with the highest current value; on a tie, the one listed first.
4. Subtract the total weight of all servers that took part from the picked server's value.

Drained servers take part in nothing: their weight is not added and does not count towards
the total.

## Worked example: a=5, b=1, c=1

| Request | After adding weights (a, b, c) | Picked | After subtracting 7 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 5, 1, 1 | a | -2, 1, 1 |
| 2 | 3, 2, 2 | a | -4, 2, 2 |
| 3 | 1, 3, 3 | b | 1, -4, 3 |
| 4 | 6, -3, 4 | a | -1, -3, 4 |
| 5 | 4, -2, 5 | c | 4, -2, -2 |
| 6 | 9, -1, -1 | a | 2, -1, -1 |
| 7 | 7, 0, 0 | a | 0, 0, 0 |

After seven requests every value is back at 0 and the cycle repeats: a a b a c a a.

# Workspace URLs are /w/<slug>. Turn a workspace name into its slug:
# lowercase ASCII letters and digits, words joined by single hyphens.
def slugify(name)

end

The service every client talks to for sign-up, login, sessions and password resets. Most of it is Go, a few older endpoints are still PHP, the admin back office is a small Ruby app, the password service is Java, and the login gateway in front is TypeScript.

Jo forwarded this from the help desk:

> I got locked out after a few wrong passwords and the page said **"Too many attempts. Try again in 0 minutes."** So I tried again straight away, and it locked me out again.

`retryMessage($secondsLeft)` in `src/retryMessage.php` writes the message the login form shows during a lockout. Lockouts run from one minute up to 24 hours.

- Round the time left **up**, so nobody is told to come back before the lock ends.
- Under 60 minutes (after rounding), say minutes: `Too many attempts. Try again in 1 minute.`, `Too many attempts. Try again in 15 minutes.`
- From 60 minutes on, say hours, also rounded up: `Too many attempts. Try again in 1 hour.`, `Too many attempts. Try again in 2 hours.`
- The lock can end between the check and the page render, so the seconds left can be zero or negative. Then the form says `You can try again now.`

src/retryMessage.php.text:
<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

/**
 * The message the login form shows while an account is locked out, for the seconds left on
 * the lock. Lockouts run from one minute up to 24 hours.
 */
function retryMessage(int $secondsLeft): string
{
    $minutes = intdiv($secondsLeft, 60);
    return "Too many attempts. Try again in {$minutes} minutes.";
}
